panels.title: Big questions
points: Should people always obey orders, even when the orders may be wrong?
Is witnessing war as painful as fighting in it?
How can a poem about one family speak about every war?

panels.title: Islamic foundation
panels.text: Islam teaches obedience to those in authority in what is right, and the Prophet ﷺ taught that there is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to Allah. Courage and loyalty are virtues, but leaders carry a heavy responsibility for the lives in their care.

points: People not fighting must not be targeted
The wounded must be cared for

panels.title: How does Tennyson present duty?
points: Point: Tennyson presents duty as unquestioning obedience
Evidence: 'Theirs not to reason why'
Technique: repetition of 'Theirs'; short lines
Zoom in: 'reason' is exactly what is denied them

Answer: Tennyson presents duty as obedience without question: the repeated 'Theirs not to reason why' denies the soldiers the very thing that might have saved them, so the line honours their courage while quietly exposing the cost of the order.

panels.title: Compare how Tennyson and Satyamurti present experiences of conflict.
points: Point: both poets present the cost of conflict, but from different positions
Evidence: Tennyson's 'Theirs not to reason why'; a line of the photographer's memory
Methods: public, galloping rhythm vs a private first-person voice
Analysis: commemoration of a crowd vs the conscience of one witness

Answer: Both poets present the cost of conflict, but Tennyson's galloping public rhythm ('Theirs not to reason why') commemorates hundreds of soldiers, whereas Satyamurti's private first-person voice shows one witness who cannot leave a single image behind.

panels.title: Compare how Weir and Satyamurti present memory.
points: P: both poems show memory as painful and private
E: 'your playground voice catching on the wind' / a line of the photographer's memory
M: Weir's sound image vs Satyamurti's visual image
A: the mother listens for her son; the witness cannot stop seeing

Answer: Both poets present memory as private pain far from the battlefield: Weir's mother strains to hear 'your playground voice catching on the wind', a sound image of childhood, whereas Satyamurti's photographer cannot stop seeing, so one grief listens and the other looks.

panels.title: Compare how the four poems present the enemy in war.
points: Theme: the enemy is not always the other army
Attitude: Owen bitter; Tennyson admiring; Weir grieving; Satyamurti troubled
Poetic methods: personified weather, refrain, textile imagery, a witness's voice
Structure: Owen's repeated endings vs Tennyson's charge forward

Answer: Across the four poems the enemy shifts: for Owen it is the 'merciless iced east winds', for Tennyson a 'blunder', for Weir absence itself, and for Satyamurti the memory a witness cannot escape.
